thread.title_full: 'Horrific act': Here's what politicians said about Charlie Kirk's shooting - NewsBreak

author: Ronald J. Hansen
title: 'Horrific act': Here's what politicians said about Charlie Kirk's shooting - NewsBreak
text:
By Ronald J. Hansen Stephanie Murray Laura Gersony Stacey Barchenger ,
7 hours ago
The slaying of conservative activist Charlie Kirk drew immediate bipartisan condemnation across the political spectrum and renewed pleas in some cases for an end to politically inspired violence.
An avalanche of the all-too-familiar calls for thoughts and prayers from scores of members of Congress and within Arizona politics followed within minutes of the mid-day Sept. 10 shooting at Utah Valley University.
Before the day ended — and with the assassin still at large — the conversation increasingly veered back to customary partisan rhetoric, especially for some on the right seething at the loss of a luminary.
President Donald Trump confirmed Kirk’s death on Truth Social a few hours after the shooting. Hours later, he blamed the “radical left” for the apparent assassination.
“The Great, and even Legendary, Charlie Kirk, is dead. No one understood or had the Heart of the Youth in the United States of America better than Charlie. He was loved and admired by ALL, especially me, and now, he is no longer with us. Melania and my Sympathies go out to his beautiful wife Erika, and family. Charlie, we love you!”
His video message from the Oval Office hours later included a vow to stop those who denounced Kirk’s often-divisive comments.
“It’s long past time for all Americans and the media to confront the fact that violence and murder are the tragic consequence of demonizing those with whom you disagree day after day, year after year, in the most hateful and despicable way possible,” Trump said.
“For years, those on the radical left have compared wonderful Americans like Charlie to Nazis and the world’s worst mass murderers and criminals. This kind of rhetoric is directly responsible for the terrorism that we’re seeing in our country today, and it must stop right now.”
Arizona Gov. Katie Hobbs, a Democrat, called on the public to reject violence and embrace civility.
“This horrific act is a reminder that political violence has no place in our society. Regardless of our beliefs or affiliations, resorting to violence to settle differences is never acceptable,” she said.
“Let’s not retreat into silence or hatred, but rise above violence by recommitting ourselves to the democratic principles of civil engagement and mutual respect.”
Vice President JD Vance said Kirk was a “genuinely good guy and a young father.” Vance and Kirk were longtime allies.
“Dear God, protect Charlie in his darkest hour,” Vance wrote before Kirk succumbed to his injury. He shared a photo of himself, Kirk and Donald Trump Jr.
U.S. Sen. Mark Kelly, D-Arizona, whose wife, former Rep. Gabrielle Giffords, D-Arizona, was shot in the head in 2011 near Tucson, called the shooting “shocking and horrible.” He said political violence seems to be a growing problem.
“We’ve seen this throughout our history, but I do feel, like many Americans, that this has gotten worse,” Kelly said in an interview with CNN.
“It’s up to us, people like myself as a United States senator, to set an example, and others need to do that as well. We’ve got to bring the temperature down and convince people that we are one nation and we are stronger when we work together.”
Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Arizona, reminded people that Kirk was more than a political figure.
“Beyond politics Charlie Kirk was someone’s father, husband and son. Remember that first, before engaging in whataboutism. His family will never be the same. Political violence has to stop by all sides,” he said.
While the assassin’s identity remained unknown, some conservatives seized on the shooting as reason to clamp down on the political left. Trump ally Laura Loomer offered a characteristically divisive reaction that blamed the political left.
“The Democrats cannot keep getting away with declaring open season on conservatives,” she wrote in a social media post.
“It’s time for the Trump administration to shut down, defund, & prosecute every single Leftist organization. If Charlie Kirk dies from his injuries, his life cannot be in vain,” Loomer wrote online . "We must shut these lunatic leftists down. Once and for all. The Left is a national security threat.”
Billionaire Elon Musk, who briefly served in the Trump administration, also blamed the political left for Kirk’s shooting before officials shared any information about the suspect’s identity.
“The Left is the party of murder,” Musk wrote on X , the social media platform he owns.
Rep. Pat Harrigan, R-North Carolina, similarly blamed the left even as the motive for the shooting remained unclear.
“The Left couldn’t stand 15 feet in front of Charlie and argue with his logic, so they shot him from 200 yards away instead Absolutely disgusting,” he wrote in a social media post.
U.S. Rep. Andy Biggs, R-Arizona, a close ally of Kirk and his Turning Point organizations, said Kirk left a mark on the nation.
“We have tragically lost a tremendous leader and a friend. But his most important role was as a loving husband, father, and devout Christian who shared his faith unapologetically,” Biggs said. “Charlie Kirk was an inspiration to an entire generation and will be remembered as someone who changed the course of our country.”
Biggs also shared a message from Sean Davis, the CEO of the conservative organization the Federalist, that blamed Democrats for the slaying.
“Democrats will murder you in cold blood and then object when someone rises to pray for your family.”
Former Sen. Jeff Flake, R-Arizona, struck a different tone.
He gave a speech at UVU on Sept. 9, one day before Kirk was shot there. In addition to that coincidence, Flake is a friend of Giffords and was on a baseball field in June 2017 when a gunman shot four people, including House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-Louisiana, in a rage against Republicans.
In an interview with CNN, Flake urged Americans to rise above violence and called for political leadership setting the example.
“We’ve got to do better. We’ve got to quit treating each other, those who we may be opposed to with or not agree with politically, we can’t treat them as an enemy,” he said.
“For those in the public eye and those holding public office — I’m not placing any blame on this specific issue — but we need to stop referring to those on the other side of us as evil. … Those of us in positions need to be a better example, frankly.”
Arizona state Senate President Warren Petersen, R-Gilbert, called for prayers for Kirk’s family and a rejection of violence.
“This attack serves as a sobering reminder of the dangerous consequences that arise when political disagreements cross the line into violence,” he said in a statement. “Regardless of where you stand on the political spectrum, there is never any justification for silencing someone with a bullet.”
Arizona state House Speaker Steve Montenegro, R-Goodyear, called Kirk an “American hero.”
“Charlie was a fearless voice who inspired millions with his faith, his devotion to freedom, and his conviction to defend America’s founding principles,” Montenegro said.
“This was political terrorism. Violence aimed at silencing any voices must be confronted and dealt with justly and without hesitation.”
Kari Lake, who oversees government-run media organizations for the Trump administration, grieved for the loss of a personal friend in a “sick, depraved act.”
“My heart is shattered,” she said in a statement. “He was assassinated in front of the young people he devoted his life to empowering. … Charlie was fearless and had the sharpest political instincts of anyone I’ve ever met, and he used them to shape a movement that will outlast him."
"This was a sick, depraved act — but Charlie’s legacy will not die with him," Lake said. "The next generation of American leaders will carry his torch. He fought for this country with his last breath, and his fight will never be in vain."
Some of the most prominent Democrats in Washington offered unambiguous condemnation of the shooting.
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-New York, said the “scourge of gun violence and political violence must end. The shooting of Charlie Kirk is the latest incident of this chaos and it must stop. We cannot go down this road.”
Rep. Nancy Pelosi, D-California, the former House speaker whose husband was bludgeoned in his home by a man who hoped to attack her, said the shooting was “reprehensible.”
“Political violence has absolutely no place in our nation. All Americans should pray for Charlie Kirk’s recovery and hold the entire UVU community in our hearts as they endure the trauma of this gun violence,” Pelosi said.
Rep. David Schweikert, R-Arizona, said he was “devastated to hear the news about Charlie Kirk. I want to extend my heartfelt prayers and support to Charlie and his family.”
Rep. Greg Stanton, D-Arizona, called the incident “horrifying. I’m praying hard for him, and keeping his family in my thoughts. Political violence has absolutely no place in our country.”
Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Arizona, tied Kirk’s death to a school shooting in Colorado the same day to condemn gun violence.
“Horrific gun tragedies one after another. Charlie Kirk lost his life. Not even an hour later, a school in Colorado came under fire. Communities shattered. Lives changed forever,” she said. “This is not normal and this is not acceptable. We cannot keep living like this.”
Giffords, who founded an anti-gun violence organization that bears her name, weighed in as well.
“Democratic societies will always have political disagreements, but we must never allow America to become a country that confronts those disagreements with violence,” Giffords said in a statement.
This article originally appeared on Arizona Republic: 'Horrific act': Here's what politicians said about Charlie Kirk's shooting
